claims.claim: An auto loan is a loan used to buy a vehicle: the borrower agrees to pay the amount financed plus a finance charge over a set period of time, repaid in monthly installments.
The vehicle typically secures an auto loan: the lender holds a lien on the car's title until the loan is paid in full, so the car serves as collateral.
The loan amount (amount financed) starts from the vehicle's price plus any financed features and fees, minus the down payment and trade-in.
The APR is the yearly cost of the loan expressed as a percentage, covering interest and lender fees; the FTC calls it the cost of credit on a yearly basis.

Auto loans come in two main arrangements: direct lending from a bank, credit union, or finance company, and dealer-arranged (indirect) financing in which the dealer forwards the application to lenders and typically adds a markup to the rate.

Dealer-arranged rates are generally higher because the dealer adds extra interest to the lender's buy rate for handling the financing; going directly to a bank or credit union tends to be the cheaper option.

The longer the loan term, the more the loan costs overall: long terms (72 or 84 months) lower the monthly payment but can carry higher rates and more total interest; cars lose value quickly, so long terms can leave a borrower owing more than the car is worth.

Missed auto loan payments can lead to repossession: in many states the lender can take the car without warning or a court order; after repossession the lender keeps or sells the car, and the borrower may still owe the difference (a deficiency).

The total cost of a financed vehicle is the monthly payment times the number of payments plus the down payment, and it can exceed the sticker price; both CFPB and FTC guidance advise comparing the APR, term, and total cost rather than focusing only on the monthly payment.

New and used vehicles sit at different price levels and usually carry different loan amounts; financing either one adds interest to the price, and low monthly payment offers on used cars often come with longer loan periods and higher interest rates.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether a lender must warn a borrower before repossessing the car.
positions: In many states a lender can repossess after a missed payment without a warning or a court order (CFPB)
Other states require lenders to send a notice before repossession (CFPB)
The FTC states a lender might be able to take the car without going to court or telling the borrower first (FTC)
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states the general reality — repossession can follow missed payments, in many states without prior notice — without claiming a single uniform national rule.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether dealer financing or direct lending is always cheaper.
positions: Interest rates through a dealer are generally higher because the dealer adds a markup to the buy rate (CFPB)
Bank or credit union financing tends to be the cheaper option because the markup is avoided (CFPB)
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents both as general tendencies rather than guarantees, and makes no recommendation between channels.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The average price level of used cars.
positions: Industry reports cited by the FTC estimated the average used-car price near $28,000
Used-car prices vary widely by vehicle, age, mileage, and market
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson keeps the new-versus-used section at the level of general price differences and attributes the $28,000 figure to industry reports as cited by the FTC, without treating it as a precise current statistic.

sourceRecords.title: Auto Loans (CFPB consumer-tools hub)
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via HTTP on 2026-08-21. The hub frames auto loans as vehicle-purchase loans, lays out the steps for getting an auto loan (know before you shop, see the ways to get a loan, know what is negotiable, close the deal), and lists common problems (owing more than the car is worth, missed payments, repossession). Supports the working definition and the lesson's structure.

sourceRecords.title: What is the difference between dealer-arranged and bank financing? (Ask CFPB)
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via HTTP on 2026-08-21. Explains indirect (dealer-arranged) financing, the buy rate plus dealer markup, that dealer rates are generally higher, that bank or credit union financing tends to be cheaper, and defines interest rate versus APR; also lists the TILA disclosures. Supports the dealer-versus-bank section and the APR definition.

sourceRecords.title: How much can I afford to borrow for a car or auto loan? (Ask CFPB)
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via HTTP on 2026-08-21. Lists what adds to the loan amount (vehicle price, optional features, taxes and fees) and what reduces it (down payment, trade-in), names the interest rate and length of the loan as cost drivers, and warns against pricing the loan off the list price alone. Supports the five-parts section, the loan-amount definition, and total-cost thinking.

sourceRecords.title: What happens if my car is repossessed? (Ask CFPB)
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via HTTP on 2026-08-21. States that in many states a lender can repossess a vehicle after a missed payment without a warning or a court order, while other states require notice, and covers borrower rights. Supports the collateral-and-repossession section as the honest note.

sourceRecords.title: Financing or Leasing a Car
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via HTTP on 2026-08-21. Defines direct lending versus dealership financing, calls the APR the cost of credit on a yearly basis, warns that total cost depends on the negotiated price, the APR, and the length of the loan rather than the monthly payment, notes that 72- and 84-month loans lower payments but raise total cost, and states the lender holds a lien on the title until the contract is paid in full. Backbone source for the mechanics, the collateral angle, and the reality check.

sourceRecords.title: Vehicle Repossession
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via HTTP on 2026-08-21. Explains that a lender may take the car without going to court or telling the borrower first after missed payments, that the lender keeps or sells the car after repossession, that a deficiency can remain, and that contacting the lender early is the recommended first step. Supports the honest note on repossession.

sourceRecords.title: Buying a Used Car from a Dealer
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via HTTP on 2026-08-21. Notes that industry reports put the average used-car price near $28,000, states that financing increases the total cost of a car because of the cost of credit including interest, and warns that low monthly payment offers often have longer loan periods and higher interest rates. Supports the new-versus-used section and the reality check.
